# Summary of Political Manifesto

This manifesto presents a vision for national governance focused on several key policy areas, emphasising action over rhetoric and accountability in government.

## Economic Policy

The document advocates for fiscal responsibility, arguing that government spending has become excessive and unsustainable. It proposes £12 billion in annual savings through reducing civil service posts and cutting public bodies. Of these savings, £8 billion would reduce borrowing while £4 billion would fund tax cuts. The manifesto commits to maintaining central bank independence for interest rate decisions and opposes adopting a common European currency.

Pensioner support features prominently, including proposals to halve council tax for over-65s, increase state pensions in line with earnings rather than prices, and create new savings accounts with government contributions.

## Education

The manifesto emphasises school discipline as fundamental to effective learning. It proposes giving head teachers full control over admissions and expulsions, with disruptive pupils directed to specialist schools. Teachers would receive protection from malicious allegations and reduced paperwork.

Funding would follow pupils, allowing parental choice to drive resources. The document proposes 600,000 additional school places, vocational grants for teenagers, and scrapping university tuition fees. It advocates for rigorous examination standards and curriculum reform.

## Healthcare

Healthcare spending would increase to £2,000 per head annually. The manifesto proposes abolishing centrally-set targets, reducing administrative bodies, and giving hospitals freedom over staffing and investment. Patients and GPs would choose care providers, with funding following patient choices. Infection control receives particular attention, with proposals to reinstate ward matrons with authority to close wards for cleaning.

## Crime and Security

The document proposes recruiting 5,000 additional police officers annually, establishing elected local police commissioners, and implementing zero-tolerance neighbourhood policing. Prison capacity would expand by 20,000 places, with sentences served in full. Drug treatment programmes would expand significantly, including 25,000 residential rehabilitation places.

## Immigration

The manifesto proposes establishing a unified border control force, implementing 24-hour port surveillance, and introducing an Australian-style points system for work permits. It advocates withdrawing from certain international agreements to establish national control over asylum policy, processing applications outside the country, and setting annual immigration limits determined by parliament.

## Governance and Constitutional Matters

Proposals include abolishing regional assemblies, returning powers to local authorities, reducing parliamentary seats by 20 per cent, and ensuring that legislation affecting only one constituent nation is decided by representatives from that nation alone. The manifesto commits to reforming the upper legislative chamber through increased elected membership.

## Foreign Policy and Defence

Defence spending would increase by £2.7 billion for front-line forces. The document opposes a proposed European constitutional treaty, promising a referendum within six months, and commits to negotiating return of certain regulatory powers from European institutions. International development spending would increase toward 0.7 per cent of national income by 2013.

## Environment and Transport

Environmental proposals include phasing out harmful chemicals, incentivising low-emission vehicles, protecting green belt land, and promoting brownfield development. Transport policy includes modernising road networks, reviewing speed cameras, and extending rail franchises to encourage private investment.

The manifesto concludes by presenting specific actions for implementation within the first day and month of taking office, emphasising immediate accountability for stated commitments.

# Summary of 2005 Policy Manifesto

This manifesto outlines a comprehensive policy platform centred on environmental sustainability, social equity, and democratic reform.

## Economic Policy

The document advocates for wealth redistribution through progressive taxation, with higher rates on upper incomes and corporate profits. It proposes replacing Value Added Tax with environmental taxes based on resource usage and pollution. A Land Value Tax would replace existing property taxes. The manifesto supports economic localisation through community banks, credit unions, and local currencies, while opposing adoption of a single European currency. It emphasises measuring wellbeing beyond traditional economic indicators.

## Energy and Climate

The manifesto adopts a "Contraction and Convergence" framework for emissions reduction, targeting 20% reduction by 2010 and 85% by 2030. Policies include a carbon tax, increasing renewable energy to 40% by 2020, implementing energy efficiency programmes, and phasing out nuclear power. A dedicated cabinet position for climate policy coordination is proposed.

## Welfare Reform

Central to the welfare proposals is a universal "Citizen's Income" providing unconditional basic income to all residents, replacing means-tested benefits. A "Citizen's Pension" would provide guaranteed retirement income linked to average earnings, eliminating means-testing. Additional measures include simplified child benefits, reduced working hours, and increased affordable housing through reformed land ownership and local authority investment.

## Public Services

Healthcare policy focuses on returning the health service to founding principles of universal comprehensive care, opposing privatisation and public-private partnerships. The manifesto proposes abolishing prescription charges, restoring free eye and dental care, and increasing funding to European average levels. Education priorities include scrapping tuition fees, restoring maintenance grants, abolishing standardised testing for younger pupils, and increasing overall funding.

## Transport

Transport policy prioritises public transport, walking, and cycling over private vehicles. Proposals include returning rail and underground networks to public ownership, extending congestion charging, increasing fuel duties, and taxing aviation fuel. The manifesto targets a 10% reduction in road traffic by 2010, redirecting road-building funds to public transport improvements.

## Environment

A "Zero Waste Strategy" would aim for 60% domestic waste recycling by 2010, banning incineration and establishing a dedicated agency for resource recovery. The manifesto applies precautionary principles to new technologies including genetic modification, opposes patents on natural resources, and strengthens animal welfare protections including banning live animal exports.

## Food and Agriculture

Agricultural policy proposes replacing European agricultural subsidies with support for organic farming and local food markets, targeting 30% organic production by 2012. The manifesto opposes genetically modified food and seeks to address anti-competitive behaviour by major retailers.

## Crime and Justice

Crime reduction focuses on community-based prevention, improved urban design, increased community policing, and youth facilities. The manifesto proposes stricter gun control legislation and expanded restorative justice programmes as alternatives to imprisonment.

## Democratic Reform

Constitutional proposals include opposing identity cards, introducing proportional representation for all elections, reforming regional government, establishing an elected upper chamber, and creating a written constitution. The manifesto opposes the proposed European constitutional treaty while supporting continued European engagement.

## International Policy

Foreign policy emphasises peaceful diplomacy, nuclear disarmament, reduced military spending, and increased overseas aid to 1% of national income. The manifesto supports cancelling debts of the poorest countries, reforming international institutions including the United Nations, and replacing current trade organisation rules with agreements prioritising sustainability and local economies over global trade expansion.
